titlePlain: Optimal Iteration Count — and Why More Isn't
subtitle: Lesson 18 · Grover's Algorithm

eyebrow: A specific number, not a range

steps.label: t* = ⌊π/(4α)⌋ ≈ ⌊(π/4)√N⌋
steps.sub: Each iteration rotates by a fixed angle 2α, with sin(α) = 1/√N

steps.label: Too few iterations: you haven't gotten there yet
steps.sub: Too many: you've swung past the marked state

steps.label: This is the single iteration count maximizing P(marked)
steps.sub: Not a "do at least this many" floor

steps.label: t* scales as √N — the source of the quadratic speedup
steps.sub: A million-fold larger space needs only ~785 iterations, not a million

code:
Iter 0: P(marked) = 0.1250  (baseline guess)
Iter 1: P(marked) = 0.7812
Iter 2: P(marked) = 0.9453  <- peak, t* = floor((pi/4)*sqrt(8)) = 2
Iter 3: P(marked) = 0.3301  (overshoot)
Iter 4: P(marked) = 0.0122  (worse than guessing!)
caption: Iteration 4's 1.22% is worse than doing zero iterations at all (12.5%) — two extra "safety" iterations actively destroy the result.

steps.label: Unlike gradient descent, there's no fixed point
steps.sub: The state keeps rotating past the marked state, around, and back

steps.label: The rotation angle 2α is constant every iteration
steps.sub: Not shrinking — this is what makes the trajectory periodic

steps.label: You must compute t* in advance
steps.sub: "Run a few more to be safe" can land you near 0% instead of near 95%

steps.label: N = 1,000,000 → t* = 785, exactly
steps.sub: Overshoot that and risk the same collapse seen at N=8
